bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Geopolitical and social risk — Rated High priority in the Board's key-risk register. Geopolitical tensions, trade restrictions or social disruptions may impact supply chains, input availability and cross-border sourcing, affecting production continuity, costs and customer fulfilment timelines. The MD&A adds that the escalation of the Middle East conflict and security concerns around key maritime trade routes disrupted energy supplies and trade routes, raising volatility in energy prices, freight rates and logistics costs. Mitigated by broadening the supplier and distributor network, dedicated market/product teams, a 'Different Models for Different Channels' approach and insurance coverage.
- Supply chain vulnerability and component availability — The MD&A lists supply chain vulnerabilities arising from material shortages, geopolitical uncertainties, logistics disruptions and natural disasters as a key market restraint that can impact component availability, extend lead times and increase operating costs. The MD&A also records a sharp, industry-wide increase in memory prices driven by supply rationalisation, capacity constraints and AI/data-centre demand, illustrating how input scarcity transmits directly into the cost structures and inventory cycles of EMS providers.
- Increase in commodity prices and forex fluctuation — Both rated High priority. Volatility in foreign exchange rates and commodity prices may impact input costs and financial performance, affecting profitability and cost competitiveness. Mitigated by strengthening internal control frameworks for data integrity and process efficiency and by timely, accurate financial and non-financial reporting.
- Threats from competition and pricing pressure — Rated High priority. Rising competition from domestic and global manufacturers may pressure pricing, margins and market share, while shifts in customer preferences may affect the continuity of customer engagements and order volumes. The MD&A reinforces this structurally: the presence of a large number of EMS providers across geographies limits pricing power and impacts revenue potential. Mitigated through R&D-led differentiation, strategic alliances and joint ventures, and talent retention.
- Talent retention and manpower attrition — Rated High priority. Shortages of skilled workforce may impact manufacturing efficiency, quality outcomes and capacity ramp-ups, affecting the ability to scale operations in line with customer requirements. The MD&A flags skilled talent availability as a critical industry-wide concern, with competition for experienced engineering, R&D, technical and sales professionals driving shortages and higher attrition.
- Succession planning — Rated High priority. Inadequate leadership succession at critical roles may disrupt strategic execution and operational stability, impacting decision-making continuity and long-term organisational resilience. Mitigated through clear policies and succession plans for all key personnel and targeted training for middle and senior management.
- Operational inefficiencies and contractual default — Both rated High priority. Process, system or capacity inefficiencies may lead to higher costs, delays or quality issues, impacting productivity and customer satisfaction; failure to meet contractual obligations due to operational, supply or financial constraints may lead to penalties or loss of customer confidence, affecting long-term customer relationships in a business built on anchor-customer contracts.
- Regulatory compliance risk — Rated High priority. Evolving regulatory requirements and inadequate internal controls may result in compliance gaps, penalties or operational disruptions, impacting business continuity and reputation. The MD&A notes that regulatory compliance is becoming increasingly complex, with EMS providers required to adhere to diverse safety, labour, environmental and trade regulations across multiple jurisdictions.
- Cybersecurity, data and intellectual property risk — Cybersecurity & Data Risk is rated High priority and sits in the Board's key-risk list alongside strategic, credit, liquidity, market, operational, reputational, legal and compliance, and ethics and conduct risks. The MD&A adds that intellectual property risk remains a key EMS concern because increasing outsourcing requires providers to implement robust legal, cybersecurity and data protection measures over customer designs.

outlook.title: Strategy & capital allocation

outlook.body: Dixon is expanding capacity across most of its verticals while pushing backward integration into components. In Mobile Phones, a 1 Million sq. ft. Noida facility is being developed for an anchor customer and will provide significant additional capacity, and the Company continues to engage with global smartphone ODMs for further manufacturing opportunities. In IT Hardware, mass production of laptops and AIOs has been established at the Chennai facility (annual production capacity of 2.5 Million units) and a new facility is being developed adjacent to the existing Chennai facility, which — with the 60:40 Inventec JV — will facilitate a foray into servers and accelerate backward integration into SSD modules, mechanicals and power supplies. In Home Appliances, the Tirupati expansion will increase annual capacity from approximately 0.6 Million units to 0.9 Million units, robotic vacuum-cleaner production has commenced through the Eureka Forbes relationship, and the Company is venturing into dishwashers, microwaves and kitchen chimneys. In Refrigerators, annual capacity has already been increased from approximately 1.2 Million to 2 Million units, and the refrigerator facility is being expanded by approximately 375,000 sq. ft. to allow manufacture of two-door refrigerators, deep freezers, Visi coolers and side-by-side refrigerators. In Consumer Electronics, the Company has invested in a state-of-the-art CKD robotic LCM line for large-size IFPDs and signage and entered the premium Mini-LED TV segment. In the Emerging Businesses, the display facility construction has been completed with machinery installation underway and mass production expected to kick start during 2026-27 under ECMS approvals granted to Dixon Display Technologies (30th March, 2026) in collaboration with HKC Overseas; camera-module capacity is being scaled from approximately 70 Million units to 180–190 Million units following the 51% acquisition of Kunshan Q Tech Microelectronics (India), which along with Dixon Electroconnect received MeitY ECMS approval on 2nd January, 2026 for camera module sub-assembly and optical transceiver-SFP respectively. In Wearables & Hearables, a new manufacturing facility is being established in Chennai for the Rexxam-Dixon AC-PCB component business, strategically located close to the anchor customer. Inorganic and structural steps during the year included the Inventec JV (Dixon IT Devices, closed 18th October 2025), the Signify lighting JV (closed 1st August 2025), the Longcheer JV through Dixtel Infocom (closed 3rd March 2026), the HKC Overseas share subscription in Dixon Display Technologies, and IsmartU India's asset purchase agreement with KHY Electronic India for a total consideration of ₹121 Crores excluding applicable taxes. At the Group level Dixon operates 30 manufacturing facilities across India, along with 9 Centres of Excellence and 5 R&D Centres.
outlook.title: Capex & expansion plans

outlook.body:
- Management believes the underlying fundamentals of the business remain strong and that low leverage, healthy return ratios, a negative working-capital cycle and a strong balance sheet provide the flexibility to invest through the cycle
- Management remains confident in the long-term India electronics manufacturing opportunity, supported by global supply-chain diversification, increasing localisation, supportive government policies and PLI/ECMS-led investments, providing Dixon a strong multi-year runway for sustainable and profitable growth
- Mobile remains the largest and most important business and continues to be a significant growth driver, with strong structural growth in the Indian smartphone manufacturing ecosystem despite short-term volatility
- Management expects a significant increase in mobile volumes, supported by exports of feature phones and smartphones, particularly for the African market
- By the end of the year the memory supply-demand situation had started to become more balanced and customer ordering patterns were showing signs of improvement
- Telecom & Networking has emerged as one of the highest-growth verticals, benefiting from structural growth in home broadband, network infrastructure, CPE devices, IPTV and 5G Fixed Wireless Access; management sees it as a multi-year growth opportunity that can become one of the largest contributors after Mobile
- IT Hardware is at an inflection point and is poised to capture a significant share of the Indian IT hardware market, supported by strong customer relationships, significant order visibility, government support for domestic manufacturing and increasing localisation
- Home Appliances is evolving into a diversified and scalable growth platform supported by strong customer relationships, expanding manufacturing capabilities and increasing ODM content
- Refrigerator demand was temporarily affected by the industry transition to revised BEE and energy-efficiency norms, which disrupted procurement and inventory patterns; 50-litre and 100-litre mini-bar capacity is fully booked and a 170-litre low-cost export refrigerator has received encouraging traction

risks.note: Rated High priority in the Board's key-risk register. Geopolitical tensions, trade restrictions or social disruptions may impact supply chains, input availability and cross-border sourcing, affecting production continuity, costs and customer fulfilment timelines. The MD&A adds that the escalation of the Middle East conflict and security concerns around key maritime trade routes disrupted energy supplies and trade routes, raising volatility in energy prices, freight rates and logistics costs. Mitigated by broadening the supplier and distributor network, dedicated market/product teams, a 'Different Models for Different Channels' approach and insurance coverage.

The MD&A lists supply chain vulnerabilities arising from material shortages, geopolitical uncertainties, logistics disruptions and natural disasters as a key market restraint that can impact component availability, extend lead times and increase operating costs. The MD&A also records a sharp, industry-wide increase in memory prices driven by supply rationalisation, capacity constraints and AI/data-centre demand, illustrating how input scarcity transmits directly into the cost structures and inventory cycles of EMS providers.

Rated High priority. Inadequate leadership succession at critical roles may disrupt strategic execution and operational stability, impacting decision-making continuity and long-term organisational resilience. Mitigated through clear policies and succession plans for all key personnel and targeted training for middle and senior management.

Both rated High priority. Process, system or capacity inefficiencies may lead to higher costs, delays or quality issues, impacting productivity and customer satisfaction; failure to meet contractual obligations due to operational, supply or financial constraints may lead to penalties or loss of customer confidence, affecting long-term customer relationships in a business built on anchor-customer contracts.

Rated High priority. In Wearables & Hearables, a new manufacturing facility is being established in Chennai for the Rexxam-Dixon AC-PCB component business, strategically located close to the anchor customer. Inorganic and structural steps during the year included the Inventec JV (Dixon IT Devices, closed 18th October 2025), the Signify lighting JV (closed 1st August 2025), the Longcheer JV through Dixtel Infocom (closed 3rd March 2026), the HKC Overseas share subscription in Dixon Display Technologies, and IsmartU India's asset purchase agreement with KHY Electronic India for a total consideration of ₹121 Crores excluding applicable taxes. At the Group level Dixon operates 30 manufacturing facilities across India, along with 9 Centres of Excellence and 5 R&D Centres.

risks.note: Rated High priority in the Board's key-risk register. Geopolitical tensions, trade restrictions or social disruptions may impact supply chains, input availability and cross-border sourcing, affecting production continuity, costs and customer fulfilment timelines. The MD&A adds that the escalation of the Middle East conflict and security concerns around key maritime trade routes disrupted energy supplies and trade routes, raising volatility in energy prices, freight rates and logistics costs. Mitigated by broadening the supplier and distributor network, dedicated market/product teams, a 'Different Models for Different Channels' approach and insurance coverage.

risks.risk: Supply chain vulnerability and component availability
risks.note: The MD&A lists supply chain vulnerabilities arising from material shortages, geopolitical uncertainties, logistics disruptions and natural disasters as a key market restraint that can impact component availability, extend lead times and increase operating costs. The MD&A also records a sharp, industry-wide increase in memory prices driven by supply rationalisation, capacity constraints and AI/data-centre demand, illustrating how input scarcity transmits directly into the cost structures and inventory cycles of EMS providers.

risks.risk: Increase in commodity prices and forex fluctuation
risks.note: Both rated High priority. Volatility in foreign exchange rates and commodity prices may impact input costs and financial performance, affecting profitability and cost competitiveness. Mitigated by strengthening internal control frameworks for data integrity and process efficiency and by timely, accurate financial and non-financial reporting.

risks.risk: Threats from competition and pricing pressure
risks.note: Rated High priority. Rising competition from domestic and global manufacturers may pressure pricing, margins and market share, while shifts in customer preferences may affect the continuity of customer engagements and order volumes. The MD&A reinforces this structurally: the presence of a large number of EMS providers across geographies limits pricing power and impacts revenue potential. Mitigated through R&D-led differentiation, strategic alliances and joint ventures, and talent retention.

Rated High priority. Shortages of skilled workforce may impact manufacturing efficiency, quality outcomes and capacity ramp-ups, affecting the ability to scale operations in line with customer requirements. The MD&A flags skilled talent availability as a critical industry-wide concern, with competition for experienced engineering, R&D, technical and sales professionals driving shortages and higher attrition.

Rated High priority. Inadequate leadership succession at critical roles may disrupt strategic execution and operational stability, impacting decision-making continuity and long-term organisational resilience. Mitigated through clear policies and succession plans for all key personnel and targeted training for middle and senior management.

Both rated High priority. Process, system or capacity inefficiencies may lead to higher costs, delays or quality issues, impacting productivity and customer satisfaction; failure to meet contractual obligations due to operational, supply or financial constraints may lead to penalties or loss of customer confidence, affecting long-term customer relationships in a business built on anchor-customer contracts.

Rated High priority. Evolving regulatory requirements and inadequate internal controls may result in compliance gaps, penalties or operational disruptions, impacting business continuity and reputation. The MD&A notes that regulatory compliance is becoming increasingly complex, with EMS providers required to adhere to diverse safety, labour, environmental and trade regulations across multiple jurisdictions.

risks.risk: Cybersecurity, data and intellectual property risk
risks.note: Cybersecurity & Data Risk is rated High priority and sits in the Board's key-risk list alongside strategic, credit, liquidity, market, operational, reputational, legal and compliance, and ethics and conduct risks. The MD&A adds that intellectual property risk remains a key EMS concern because increasing outsourcing requires providers to implement robust legal, cybersecurity and data protection measures over customer designs.

one_liner.title: One Liner (RHP)
one_liner.body: Dixon Technologies is one of India's leading Electronic Manufacturing Services (EMS) providers, operating 30 manufacturing facilities across India as an OEM and ODM for global and domestic consumer electronics, appliance and technology brands.

business_model.title: What they do
business_model.body: Dixon integrates design, engineering and large-scale manufacturing to deliver end-to-end manufacturing solutions across the product lifecycle for leading consumer electronics, appliance and technology brands, operating as both an Original Equipment Manufacturer (OEM) and an Original Design Manufacturer (ODM). The Group operates across Mobile Phones, Consumer Electronics, Home Appliances & Engineering, Refrigerators, Telecom & Networking Products, IT Hardware, Wearables & Hearables and Emerging Businesses (displays, camera modules). It runs a B2B model serving brand customers, and is progressing beyond assembly into complex component manufacturing through backward integration, localisation and joint ventures.

demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- Management believes the underlying fundamentals of the business remain strong and that low leverage, healthy return ratios, a negative working-capital cycle and a strong balance sheet provide the flexibility to invest through the cycle
- Management remains confident in the long-term India electronics manufacturing opportunity, supported by global supply-chain diversification, increasing localisation, supportive government policies and PLI/ECMS-led investments, providing Dixon a strong multi-year runway for sustainable and profitable growth
- Mobile remains the largest and most important business and continues to be a significant growth driver, with strong structural growth in the Indian smartphone manufacturing ecosystem despite short-term volatility
- Management expects a significant increase in mobile volumes, supported by exports of feature phones and smartphones, particularly for the African market
- By the end of the year the memory supply-demand situation had started to become more balanced and customer ordering patterns were showing signs of improvement
- Telecom & Networking has emerged as one of the highest-growth verticals, benefiting from structural growth in home broadband, network infrastructure, CPE devices, IPTV and 5G Fixed Wireless Access; management sees it as a multi-year growth opportunity that can become one of the largest contributors after Mobile
- IT Hardware is at an inflection point and is poised to capture a significant share of the Indian IT hardware market, supported by strong customer relationships, significant order visibility, government support for domestic manufacturing and increasing localisation
- Home Appliances is evolving into a diversified and scalable growth platform supported by strong customer relationships, expanding manufacturing capabilities and increasing ODM content
- Refrigerator demand was temporarily affected by the industry transition to revised BEE and energy-efficiency norms, which disrupted procurement and inventory patterns; 50-litre and 100-litre mini-bar capacity is fully booked and a 170-litre low-cost export refrigerator has received encouraging traction
- The Indian lighting industry is going through consolidation as smaller players struggle to invest in technology, quality and compliance, which management sees as a share-gain opportunity for a well-capitalised, integrated platform
- Headwinds during the year: significant inflation in key components, particularly memory chips and semiconductor-linked inputs driven by AI and data-centre demand, causing supply constraints and higher input costs; geopolitical tensions, supply-chain and freight disruptions, energy and commodity-price volatility, currency movements, softer consumer demand and inventory rationalisation by brands, with smartphones and IT Hardware particularly affected
- Industry context: the Indian EMS market, valued at approximately US$ 40-45 Billion in 2024-25, is projected to surpass US$ 150 Billion by 2029-30, growing at a CAGR of over 25%
- Industry context: India's electronics manufacturing market is estimated at around US$130 Billion in 2025 with projections of approximately US$415 Billion by 2030; mobile phones have moved from India's 153rd-largest export item in 2014-15 to its single largest export product in 2025-26
- Policy tailwind: the Government of India increased funding for the Electronics Components Manufacturing Scheme (ECMS) to INR 40,000 Crores in the Union Budget 2026-27, with a larger goal of a $500 billion electronics manufacturing industry by 2030-31 and 25% of production expected to be outsourced
- Telecom & Networking: strong relationships with anchor customers and a continuing healthy order pipeline
- Home Appliances: production of robotic vacuum cleaners has commenced through the Eureka Forbes relationship and the Company has a healthy order book
- Wearables & Hearables: the business has a healthy order book alongside strong margins and good ROCE
- IT Hardware: significant order visibility cited alongside strong customer relationships
- Lighting: orders received from major US and European retail chains, with additional international opportunities being explored
- Refrigerators: 50-litre and 100-litre mini-bar capacity has been fully booked

capex_expansion.title: Capex & expansion plans
capex_expansion.body: Dixon is expanding capacity across most of its verticals while pushing backward integration into components. In Mobile Phones, a 1 Million sq. ft. Noida facility is being developed for an anchor customer and will provide significant additional capacity, and the Company continues to engage with global smartphone ODMs for further manufacturing opportunities. In IT Hardware, mass production of laptops and AIOs has been established at the Chennai facility (annual production capacity of 2.5 Million units) and a new facility is being developed adjacent to the existing Chennai facility, which — with the 60:40 Inventec JV — will facilitate a foray into servers and accelerate backward integration into SSD modules, mechanicals and power supplies. In Home Appliances, the Tirupati expansion will increase annual capacity from approximately 0.6 Million units to 0.9 Million units, robotic vacuum-cleaner production has commenced through the Eureka Forbes relationship, and the Company is venturing into dishwashers, microwaves and kitchen chimneys. In Refrigerators, annual capacity has already been increased from approximately 1.2 Million to 2 Million units, and the refrigerator facility is being expanded by approximately 375,000 sq. ft. to allow manufacture of two-door refrigerators, deep freezers, Visi coolers and side-by-side refrigerators. In Consumer Electronics, the Company has invested in a state-of-the-art CKD robotic LCM line for large-size IFPDs and signage and entered the premium Mini-LED TV segment. In the Emerging Businesses, the display facility construction has been completed with machinery installation underway and mass production expected to kick start during 2026-27 under ECMS approvals granted to Dixon Display Technologies (30th March, 2026) in collaboration with HKC Overseas; camera-module capacity is being scaled from approximately 70 Million units to 180–190 Million units following the 51% acquisition of Kunshan Q Tech Microelectronics (India), which along with Dixon Electroconnect received MeitY ECMS approval on 2nd January, 2026 for camera module sub-assembly and optical transceiver-SFP respectively. In Wearables & Hearables, a new manufacturing facility is being established in Chennai for the Rexxam-Dixon AC-PCB component business, strategically located close to the anchor customer. Inorganic and structural steps during the year included the Inventec JV (Dixon IT Devices, closed 18th October 2025), the Signify lighting JV (closed 1st August 2025), the Longcheer JV through Dixtel Infocom (closed 3rd March 2026), the HKC Overseas share subscription in Dixon Display Technologies, and IsmartU India's asset purchase agreement with KHY Electronic India for a total consideration of ₹121 Crores excluding applicable taxes. At the Group level Dixon operates 30 manufacturing facilities across India, along with 9 Centres of Excellence and 5 R&D Centres.

moat.body:

- Beneficiary of 5 PLI schemes and an ECMS beneficiary across 3 categories, with ECMS approvals granted for camera-module sub-assembly, optical transceiver-SFP and display module sub-assembly

- Largest OEM and ODM company in India in Consumer Electronics, and the largest ODM solution provider of washing machines in India (Semi-Automatic and Fully Automatic Top-Load)
- Backward integration and localisation into critical components - camera modules, display modules, optical transceivers, plastic mouldings, adapters and sheet-metal parts - capturing a greater share of the electronics value chain
- Deep anchor-customer relationships and strategic partnerships/JVs with global players: Inventec (60:40, IT hardware), Signify (50:50, lighting), Imagine Marketing (50:50, wearables & hearables), Rexxam (AC-PCB), Longcheer, HKC Overseas (displays) and the 51% Q-Tech India acquisition

other.title: Notable from the deck
other.body:
- [PLI dispute] A subsidiary has recognised PLI incentive income for revenues exceeding the prescribed annual ceiling on the basis that other eligible applicants in the same target segment "have not fully utilised their respective ceiling entitlements"; Rs. 1,110.06 crores "remains outstanding and receivable as at 30 June 2026, pending formal determination and disbursement by the Project Management Agency", against which a liability of Rs. 603.95 crores payable to its customer has been recognised. The auditor drew an emphasis of matter on it, with conclusion not modified.
- [PLI basis of recognition] Recognition rests on "management's assessment of the performance of other applicants, using publicly available information and internally available data" and on "independent legal advice, which confirms the subsidiary's eligibility for incentive upon achievement of the prescribed conditions under the Scheme" - i.e. on estimates of third-party behaviour rather than on a PMA determination.
- [Audit scope] The principal auditor "did not review the interim financial results of two subsidiaries included in the Statement, whose interim financial results reflect total revenues of Rs. 2,336.50 crores, total net profit after tax of Rs. 32.21 crores and total comprehensive income of Rs. 32.27 crores, for the quarter ended 30 June 2026", relying instead on other auditors' reports.
- [Gain on divestment - conflicting figures] The standalone notes state the gain on sale of the undertaking and subsidiary shares as "Rs. 21.88 crores and Rs. 24.99 crores respectively", while the consolidated notes state "Rs. 21.88 crores and Rs. 6.19 crores respectively" - the deck carries both readings.
